content:
Public Python functions have docstrings
Every public function and class explains what it does in a docstring whose first line is an imperative sentence.

Python exceptions name the failing value
Raise exceptions with a message that quotes the value that was rejected, so a log line is enough to reproduce the failure.

Python modules use the module logger
Log through logging.getLogger(__name__) and never print from library code.

Mutable default arguments are forbidden
Use None as the default and create the list or dict inside the function body.

Files are opened in a with block
Open files and sockets in with statements so they close even when an exception passes through.

Comprehensions stay on one line
When a comprehension needs two lines, write a loop or a helper function instead.

Dataclasses hold plain records
Use a dataclass for a record with no behavior and a regular class when it validates or transforms its fields.

Enums replace magic strings
A value from a closed set of options is an Enum member, not a string compared in several places.

Paths are built with pathlib
Join and inspect filesystem paths with pathlib objects instead of concatenating strings.

Python lines are at most 100 characters
Wrap long expressions in parentheses rather than with backslashes.

Generators are preferred for large inputs
Yield items one at a time when the caller only iterates, so memory stays flat as the input grows.

Python tuples are not used as records
A record with more than three fields is a dataclass or a named tuple, never a bare tuple.

Assertions check programmer errors only
Use assert for conditions that cannot happen and raise a real exception for bad input.

Properties are cheap
A property must not do input or output; make it a method when it costs more than a lookup.

Python scripts have a main guard
Scripts put their work in a main function called under the standard main guard so they can be imported.

Test files mirror the package layout
A module at pkg/a/b.py is tested in tests/a/test_b.py so each test is easy to find.

Fixtures live in conftest.py
Shared pytest fixtures go in the nearest conftest file and never in a test module.

A test checks one behavior
Name the behavior in the test name and keep to a single reason for the test to fail.

Tests do not touch the network
Replace remote calls with a local fake server or recorded responses so the suite runs offline.

Parametrize instead of copying a test
Use pytest parametrization when only the input and the expected value change.

Temporary files use tmp_path
Tests write to the tmp_path fixture and leave nothing in the working directory.

Tests do not depend on the clock
Inject the current time or freeze it, so a test passes at any hour and on any date.

Mocks stop at the boundary
Mock the edge of the system, such as a client or a queue, and use the real objects inside it.

A failing test is fixed or removed
A test marked as expected to fail needs an issue link and an owner, and is reviewed every month.

Test data builders hide the noise
Build test objects through a helper that sets valid defaults, so each test shows only the fields it cares about.

Slow tests carry a marker
Mark tests that take more than a second so a quick run can skip them.

Assertion messages say what was expected
When a plain assert would be unclear, add a message that names the expected and the actual value.

Tests do not share state
Every test creates what it needs and can run alone and in any order.

Snapshot files are reviewed like code
A changed snapshot goes through review, and the author says why the output changed.

Regression tests name their issue
A test added for a bug carries the issue number in its docstring.

HTTP clients reuse their connections
Create one session per service and reuse it, so connections and TLS handshakes are shared between requests.

HTTP clients check the status code
Look at the status of every response before reading its body, and turn a 4xx or 5xx into a typed error.

Only idempotent requests are repeated
Automatic repeats are limited to GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE; a POST is repeated only with an idempotency key.

Redirects are followed on purpose
Follow redirects only for safe methods, and cap how many a client will follow.

TLS verification stays on
Never switch certificate verification off in code; point the client at the right trust store instead.

Response bodies are read as streams when large
Stream a download to disk in chunks instead of holding the whole body in memory.

The user agent names the client and its version
Every outgoing request sends a user agent string with the product name and its release.

Query strings are built by the library
Pass parameters as a mapping and let the client encode them, instead of formatting a URL by hand.

JSON bodies are sent with the matching header
When a request carries JSON, the content type header says so and the body is serialized once.

Proxies are read from the environment
Honor the standard proxy variables and offer one setting to turn them off for a single call.

Cookies belong to a session object
Keep cookies in the session that received them and never copy them between services.

Response encodings are not guessed twice
Trust the charset the server declares and fall back to UTF-8 only when it declares none.

Failed requests log the method and the URL path
A log line for a failure includes the method, the path without its query, and the status.

Pagination follows the link headers
Walk a paginated listing by the next link the server returns, not by counting pages.

Large uploads are sent as multipart streams
Send files as a multipart stream with their names and media types set explicitly.

API paths use plural nouns
Name a collection endpoint with a plural noun and identify a member by its id in the path.

Errors are returned as problem documents
Every error response is a JSON object with a type, a title, a status and a detail.

Status codes say what happened
Use 201 for a created resource, 204 for an empty success and 409 for a conflict, and keep 200 for a body.

API versions live in the path
Put the major version at the start of the path and never change a released response shape inside it.

Deprecations are announced in headers
A deprecated endpoint answers with a header that names its replacement and the date it goes away.

List endpoints are paginated by default
A listing without a page size returns a small default page and a link to the next one.

Filters use query parameters
Narrow a listing with named query parameters, never with a different path.

Responses carry a request id
Return the id of the request in a header so a user report can be matched to a log line.

PUT replaces and PATCH merges
A PUT sends the whole resource and a PATCH sends only the fields that change.

Rate limits are visible
Answer with the limit, the remaining calls and the reset time in the standard rate limit headers.

Caching headers are set on every GET
Send an ETag or a last modified date so clients can ask whether a response changed.

Cross-origin access is an allow list
List the origins that may call the API by name and never answer with a wildcard for credentialed requests.

OpenAPI is the source of the contract
Change the OpenAPI file first and generate the server stubs and the client from it.

Webhooks are signed
Every webhook carries a signature header that the receiver verifies before reading the body.

Idempotency keys expire
Store an idempotency key with its first response and drop it after a day.

Documents open with the reader's goal
The first paragraph says what the reader will be able to do after reading the page.

Code samples name their language
Every fenced block states its language so the page can highlight it.

Samples in the docs are run in CI
Examples are extracted and executed by the test suite, so a broken sample fails the build.

Links use descriptive text
Write the name of the target as the link text and never the words click here.

Images have alternative text
Every image carries a text that says what it shows, for readers who cannot see it.

One sentence, one idea
Split a sentence that carries two claims, and keep paragraphs to five sentences or fewer.

Commands are shown with their output
When a page shows a command, it also shows what the reader should see when it works.

Terms are defined at first use
Define a technical word where it first appears and link later uses to that definition.

Tables hold facts, not prose
Use a table for options and their values, and keep sentences out of the cells.

Warnings come before the step they affect
Put a caution above the instruction it applies to, never after it.

Pages end with the next step
Close a tutorial with a link to what to read or do next.

Docs name the version they describe
A page that depends on a release says which release at its top.

File names in docs are lowercase with dashes
Name documentation files in lowercase words separated by dashes.

Placeholders are written in capitals
Show a value the reader must replace in capital letters and explain it right below the sample.

Docs avoid the word simply
Do not call a step simple or obvious; the reader decides that.

Docs follow the four kinds of documentation
Keep tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation in separate pages.

The README answers three questions
A README says what the project is, how to install it and where to read more.

Reference docs are generated from the source
Build the API reference from docstrings so the code and the page cannot drift apart.

Every public option is documented
A configuration setting that is not in the reference does not exist for the user.

Architecture decisions are recorded
Write a short decision record for each choice that is costly to reverse, with the options that were refused.

Docs have an owner per section
Each section lists the team that keeps it up to date.

Broken links fail the docs build
The documentation build checks every internal and external link and fails on a dead one.

A glossary lives in one page
Keep the definitions of project terms in a single glossary and link to it.

Troubleshooting pages start from the error text
Title each entry with the exact message the user sees.

Docs ship with the code they describe
A pull request that changes behavior changes its documentation in the same pull request.

Diagrams are kept as text
Store diagrams in a text format that diffs well and render them during the build.

Onboarding is tested by a newcomer
Each quarter a new team member follows the setup guide and fixes what is wrong.

Deprecated pages stay reachable
Mark an old page as deprecated and link to its replacement instead of deleting it.

Docs search is checked with real queries
Keep a list of the ten most common questions and verify that search finds their answers.

Translated pages record their source version
A translation states the version of the original it was made from.

Release notes group changes by kind
Under each version, group the changes as added, changed, fixed and removed.

A release section opens with its version and date
Head each release with the version number and the date it was published.

Breaking changes come first
List breaking changes at the top of a release, each with what to do about it.

Deprecations name the removal release
A deprecation notice says in which release the feature will be removed.

Release notes are written for users
Describe a change by what it means for someone using the project, not by the files that moved.

Security fixes are labeled
Mark a fix for a vulnerability as a security fix and point to its advisory.

Pre-release builds are marked as such
A release candidate carries a suffix in its version and is never promoted without a new build.

Versions follow semantic versioning
Raise the major number for a breaking change, the minor for a feature and the patch for a fix.

Release tags are annotated
Create release tags with a message and push them in one step.

Every release has an upgrade section
Explain the steps to move from the previous release, including any data migration.

Contributors are thanked by name
Credit the people who contributed to a release in its notes.

A release is announced where users read
Publish the notes on the project page and in the channel users follow.

Yanked releases are explained
When a release is withdrawn, say why and name the release to use instead.

Release checklists are versioned
Keep the release checklist in the repository and update it when a step changes.

Release branches get only fixes
After a release branch is cut, accept bug fixes and nothing else on it.

Branch names say the kind and the topic
Name a branch with a prefix such as feature or fix, a slash and a few words.

Pull requests stay small
Keep a pull request to one idea and about four hundred changed lines.

Main is always releasable
Merge to main only what passes the full build, so any commit can be shipped.

Rebase local work, merge shared work
Rebase a private branch before opening a pull request and merge once others depend on it.

Commits are atomic
Each commit builds and passes tests on its own and holds one coherent change.

Force pushes are limited to private branches
Never force push a branch that another person may have checked out.

Large files stay out of the repository
Store binaries in object storage and keep a pointer file in the repository.

Hooks run the fast checks
Pre-commit hooks run formatting and linting and finish in a few seconds.

Reverts are plain commits
Undo a change with a revert commit that links to the original instead of rewriting history.

Tags mark every release
Tag each release commit and never move a tag once it is pushed.

Stale branches are deleted after merge
Delete a branch when its pull request is merged.

Pull request titles say what changes
Write the title as the effect of the change, in the present tense.

Drafts are used for early feedback
Open a draft pull request when the work is not ready, and mark it ready when it is.

Merge commits keep the pull request number
The merge or squash message ends with the number of the pull request.

Bisecting is possible
Keep history free of commits that do not build, so a bisect can walk through it.

Reviewers answer within one working day
Pick up a requested review within a working day or say when you will.

Review comments say why
Each comment names the problem and the reason, and suggests a fix when one is clear.

Nits are marked as nits
Prefix a purely stylistic comment with nit so the author knows it can wait.

Authors explain their pull request
The description says what changed, why, and how it was checked.

Approvals mean the reviewer ran the change
Approve only after reading the diff and, for risky changes, running it.

Large refactors are reviewed in steps
Split a refactor into moves and edits so each review step is mechanical.

Reviewers check the tests first
Start a review with the tests, because they state what the change is meant to do.

Disagreements go to a call
After two rounds of comments without agreement, talk it through and write down the outcome.

Security-sensitive changes need a second reviewer
A change to authentication or permissions needs two approvals.

Reviewers look for missing cases
Ask what happens with empty input, a failure halfway and a repeated call.

Praise is part of a review
Say what is good about a change as well as what should be different.

Self-review comes before the request
Read your own diff in the review tool before asking anyone else.

Reviews do not block on formatting
Leave formatting to the tool and keep review time for design and behavior.

Follow-up work gets its own issue
When a review finds work that is out of scope, file an issue and link it.

Reverted changes get a retrospective note
When a merged change is reverted, add a short note on what the review missed.

Tests run on every push
The full unit suite runs on each push and blocks the merge when it fails.

Flaky tests are quarantined
A test that fails at random is moved to a quarantine list within a day and fixed within a week.

Coverage is a signal, not a target
Watch the trend of coverage, and do not write tests only to raise the number.

Integration tests use real services
Run integration tests against containers of the real database and queue, not mocks.

Property tests cover parsers
Parsers and serializers get property-based tests that check a round trip.

Golden files record big outputs
Compare large outputs with a stored golden file and review any change to it.

Load tests run before a release
Run a load test on the release candidate and compare it with the last release.

Every bug fix adds a test
A fix is not done until a test fails without it and passes with it.

Test names are sentences
Name a test as a sentence that states the behavior, so a failure reads like a report.

Contract tests guard service boundaries
Services that call each other share consumer-driven contract tests.

Test environments are disposable
Create the environment for a run from scratch and destroy it afterwards.

Mutation testing checks the important modules
Run mutation testing on the billing and permission modules every month.

End-to-end tests cover the main journeys
Keep a small set of end-to-end tests for the three journeys users rely on most.

Tests run in random order
Shuffle the order of tests on every run to catch hidden dependencies.

Performance tests have budgets
A performance test states the limit it enforces and fails when the limit is passed.

Workflows pin their actions by commit
Reference a third-party action by its full commit hash, not by a moving tag.

Workflows declare minimal permissions
Set the token permissions of each job to read-only unless it must write.

Dependencies are cached by lockfile hash
Key the dependency cache on the hash of the lockfile so it refreshes when it should.

Matrix builds cover the supported platforms
Test each supported operating system and runtime in a build matrix.

Build artifacts are uploaded once
Build the package once, upload it as an artifact and reuse it in later jobs.

Deployments need a manual approval for production
A production deployment waits for an approval from an owner of the service.

Jobs have a time limit
Give every job a maximum run time so a hung step cannot hold a runner.

Scheduled workflows run at off-peak hours
Run nightly jobs in the early morning of the team's main time zone.

Workflow files are linted
Run a linter on the workflow files in the same pipeline that uses them.

Release workflows run only from tags
Publishing happens from a tag push, never from a branch.

Failures notify the author
A failed run on main notifies the person who merged it.

Reusable workflows hold shared steps
Move steps that appear in three workflows into one reusable workflow.

Environments hold deployment variables
Store per-environment settings in the environment, not in the workflow file.

Self-hosted runners are ephemeral
Start a clean runner for each job and remove it when the job ends.

Build logs are kept for a month
Retain logs and artifacts for thirty days, then expire them.

Dependencies are audited on a schedule
Run the dependency audit every week and open an issue for each finding.

Services run with the least privilege
Give each service only the permissions it uses, and review them every quarter.

Input is validated at the edge
Validate and normalize every external input where it enters the system.

SQL uses bound parameters
Pass values to a query as parameters and never build a statement from user text.

Output is escaped for its context
Escape text for HTML, for URLs and for shell commands separately, at the point of output.

State-changing requests carry a CSRF defense
Protect every browser request that changes data with a token or a same-site cookie.

Sign-in attempts are rate limited
Limit repeated failed sign-ins per account and per address, and tell the user how long to wait.

Sessions expire
A session ends after a period of inactivity and after a maximum age.

Security headers are set by default
Send content security, frame and content type headers on every page.

Uploads are scanned and size-limited
Limit the size and type of an upload and scan it before it is stored.

Admin actions are audited
Record who did what and when for every administrative action.

Encryption keys rotate
Rotate encryption keys every year and keep the old ones only to decrypt.

Threat models precede big features
Write a short threat model before building a feature that handles personal data.

Vulnerabilities are fixed by severity
Fix critical findings within two days and high ones within two weeks.

Third-party code is vetted
Check the maintainers and the activity of a library before adding it.

Logs are structured
Write logs as JSON objects with a level, a message and the fields that matter.

Log levels have meaning
Use error for what needs action, warning for what may, and info for normal events.

Every request has a trace id
Create a trace id at the edge and pass it through every service call.

Metrics names follow one pattern
Name a metric with the service, the subject and the unit, in lowercase with underscores.

Dashboards answer one question
Each dashboard has a title that states the question it answers.

Alerts point to a runbook
Every alert links to a page that says how to check and fix the problem.

Alerts page only for user impact
Wake a person only for symptoms that users feel and handle causes during the day.

Health checks test dependencies
The health endpoint checks the database and the queue and reports each separately.

Errors are grouped by fingerprint
Send exceptions to the tracker with a fingerprint so repeats are one issue.

Sampling is documented
Write down what share of traces and logs is kept and why.

Service levels are published
State the availability and latency targets of each service and report on them monthly.

Logs never hold personal data
Redact personal data from logs before they leave the process.

Clocks are synchronized
Run time synchronization on every host so timestamps from different machines line up.

Capacity is reviewed each quarter
Compare the growth of load with the capacity left and plan before it runs out.

Incidents are reviewed without blame
After an incident, write what happened and what will change, naming systems and not people.

Tables have a primary key
Every table declares a primary key, even when it is a join table.

Foreign keys are declared
Declare foreign keys in the schema so the database enforces the relation.

Index names say what they cover
Name an index with the table and the columns it covers.

Timestamps are stored with a time zone
Store moments in a type that keeps the time zone and convert only for display.

Deletes are soft for business records
Mark a business record as deleted with a timestamp and keep it for reporting.

Transactions are short
Open a transaction late and close it early, and never wait for a person inside one.

Money is stored as integers
Keep amounts in the smallest currency unit as integers, never as floats.

Queries name their columns
Select the columns you need by name instead of using a star.

Large tables are changed in batches
Update or delete millions of rows in batches, so locks stay short.

Enumerations are lookup tables
Store a closed set of values in a small table with a foreign key to it.

Unique constraints back every natural key
Enforce a natural key with a unique constraint, not only in application code.

Column names are singular and snake case
Name columns in lowercase with underscores and no table prefix.

New columns start nullable or with a default
Add a column in a form that old code can still write, then tighten it later.

Slow queries are explained before merging
Attach the query plan to a change that adds a query on a big table.

Views hide joins that repeat
Create a view for a join that three queries share.

Base images are pinned by digest
Pin a base image to its digest so a rebuild gives the same bytes.

Images are built in stages
Compile in a build stage and copy only the result into a small runtime stage.

Containers declare a health check
Each image defines a health command that the orchestrator can run.

Containers set resource limits
Give every container a memory and processor limit.

Images hold one process
Run one main process per container and let the orchestrator restart it.

Layers are ordered by how often they change
Copy the dependency list before the source so the dependency layer stays cached.

Images are scanned before they are pushed
Scan an image for known vulnerabilities in the build and block a critical one.

Containers write logs to standard output
Send logs to standard output and standard error and let the platform collect them.

Volumes hold only state
Mount a volume only for data that must survive, never for code.

Images carry labels
Label an image with its source repository, commit and build date.

Containers are stateless
Keep sessions and uploads outside the container so any copy can serve any request.

The root filesystem is read-only
Run with a read-only root filesystem and a small writable temporary directory.

Build contexts are small
Exclude build output and local tools from the build context.

Environment variables configure containers
Configure a container through environment variables set at deploy time.

Tags are immutable
Never overwrite a published image tag; publish a new one.

TypeScript runs in strict mode
Keep strict checking on in every project and fix errors instead of silencing them.

The any type is not used
Use unknown and narrow it, or write the real type.

Components are named in Pascal case
Name a component with a capitalized noun and keep one component per file.

State lives as close as possible to its use
Keep state in the component that needs it and lift it only when two siblings share it.

Effects clean up after themselves
Every effect that subscribes or starts a timer returns a cleanup function.

Interactive elements are real buttons and links
Use button and anchor elements for actions and navigation, not clickable divs.

Forms label every field
Each input has a visible label connected to it.

Color is never the only signal
Pair a color with an icon or a text so people who cannot see it get the message.

CSS classes describe purpose
Name a class for what the element is for, not for how it looks.

Media queries start from small screens
Write the base styles for narrow screens and add rules as the width grows.

Async calls handle their failure
Every request in the interface has a loading state and an error state.

Lists have stable keys
Give each item of a rendered list a key from its data, never its position.

Bundles have a size budget
Fail the build when the main bundle grows past its budget.

Dates are formatted by the locale
Format dates and numbers with the user's locale and not with a fixed pattern.

Images are sized in markup
Set the width and height of images so the page does not jump while they load.

Go packages are named in lowercase
A Go package has a short lowercase name that does not repeat its directory path.

Go contexts are passed first
A function that may block takes a context as its first parameter.

Goroutines have an owner
Whoever starts a goroutine is responsible for stopping it.

Rust avoids unwrap outside tests
Return a Result and handle it, and keep unwrap for tests and for proven invariants.

Rust types derive Debug
Derive Debug on every public type so it can appear in a log line.

Rust borrows before it clones
Pass a reference first and clone only when the owner needs its own copy.

Java classes are final by default
Make a class final unless it is designed for inheritance.

Java optionals are return types only
Return an Optional from a method, never take one as a parameter or a field.

Java resources use try with resources
Open streams and connections in try-with-resources blocks.

Interfaces are small
Define an interface with the one or two methods the caller needs.

Public APIs are documented in the source
Every exported item carries a documentation comment with an example when it helps.

Concurrency is tested with a race detector
Run the test suite under the race detector or the thread sanitizer in CI.

Build tools are pinned
Pin the compiler and build tool versions in the repository so builds match.

Benchmarks live next to the code
Keep a benchmark beside the function it measures and run it before a performance change.

Linters run with the strict profile
Enable the strict profile of the linter and treat its findings as build errors.

Shell scripts stop on the first error
Start a script with strict mode settings so a failed step ends the run.

Variables are quoted
Quote every expansion so spaces in a value do not split it.

Scripts print usage on bad input
A script prints a short usage text and exits with a nonzero status when called wrongly.

Scripts clean up their temporary files
Create temporary files with a helper and remove them in a trap on exit.

Long scripts become programs
When a script passes a hundred lines or needs data structures, rewrite it in a real language.

Scripts avoid hidden dependencies
List the tools a script needs at its top and check that they are installed.

Scripts are idempotent
Running a setup script twice leaves the machine in the same state as running it once.

Scripts take their paths as arguments
Read locations from arguments or variables and do not hard code a user's home.

Scripts log what they do
Print each major step so a failure in a pipeline can be placed.

Scripts are checked by a linter
Run a shell linter in CI on every script.

Scripts use long option names
Prefer long flags in scripts, since they read like documentation.

Destructive scripts ask first
A script that deletes data requires a confirmation flag and supports a dry run.

Exit codes carry meaning
Use distinct nonzero exit codes for usage errors and for runtime failures.

Scripts do not parse tool output by eye
Ask a tool for machine readable output instead of cutting its text.

Cron jobs write to a log
Every scheduled script records its start, its end and its result.

Estimates are ranges
Give an estimate as a range with the assumptions behind it.

Issues have acceptance criteria
Every issue says how we will know it is done.

Meetings have notes with decisions
Share notes after a meeting listing decisions, owners and dates.

Work in progress is limited
A person has at most two items in progress, and finishes one before pulling another.

Bugs have steps to reproduce
A bug report lists the steps, the expected result and the actual result.

Incidents have one commander
During an incident one person coordinates and others report to them.

Priorities are ranked, not tagged
Order the backlog in a single list instead of marking everything as urgent.

Proposals are written before big work
For work longer than two weeks, circulate a one page proposal first.

Demos happen every sprint
Show working software to stakeholders at the end of each sprint.

Decisions are made in writing
Record a decision in the tracker or the decision log, not only in chat.

On-call handovers are written
The person leaving on-call writes what is open, what is risky and what to watch.

Retrospectives produce at most three actions
Pick up to three actions from a retrospective and review them at the next one.

Support questions become documentation
When a question is asked twice, answer it in the docs and link there.

Scope changes update the plan
When the scope changes, change the plan and tell the people who depend on it.

Technical debt is tracked as issues
Record debt as an issue with its cost and the trigger to pay it.

Measure before optimizing
Profile the program and fix the biggest cost first, not the one that looks slow.

N plus one queries are removed
Load related records in one query or a join, not in a loop.

Caches have an invalidation rule
Write down what clears each cache entry before adding the cache.

Feature flags have an owner and a date
Each flag names who removes it and by when.

Configuration is validated at startup
Load and check every setting at startup and refuse to run with a bad one.

Settings are read from the environment
Services read their settings from environment variables with documented names.

Defaults are safe
A setting that is missing leaves the system in its safest mode.

Background jobs are retried with backoff
Retry a failed job with a growing delay and a limit, then move it to a dead letter queue.

Batch sizes are configurable
Expose the size of a batch as a setting so it can be tuned without a release.

Memory use has a ceiling
Cap the size of in-process caches and buffers.

Startup time is watched
Track how long a service takes to become ready and investigate when it doubles.

Pagination protects the database
Cap the page size a client can ask for and page by a key, not an offset.

Compression is applied to large payloads
Compress responses and stored blobs above a size threshold.

Cold paths are not optimized
Leave rarely used code simple and spend effort on the paths users hit all the time.

Resource pools are sized by measurement
Set connection and thread pool sizes from load tests and revisit them after big changes.
